content: These guidelines emphasize keeping air lead levels as low as possible to protect future generations. Additionally, the use of lead glazing in pottery intended for cooking, eating, or drinking should be discontinued. Radon, which decays by emitting alpha particles, can also originate from building materials containing radionuclides such as radium-226, thorium-232, and potassium-40. Housing in areas with previous radon mining activities poses additional risks. WHO also provides resources on safe and effective methods for controlling lead-based paint hazards. The WHO Handbook on Indoor Radon (2009) offers practical guidance on radon management, including prevention in new buildings and mitigation in existing ones. Combining these strategies often yields the most effective reduction in radon concentrations. National radon policies should identify high-risk geographic areas and raise public awareness about radon’s health risks. These policies should include training for building professionals and stakeholders involved in radon prevention and mitigation. WHO emphasizes the importance of addressing housing-related health risks through evidence-based guidelines. These guidelines aim to achieve optimal housing standards that promote health and well-being. However, implementation varies by country due to differences in resources, feasibility, and priorities. Effective implementation requires coordination among national, regional, and local governments, as well as collaboration between public, private, and civil society actors. Interventions may include structural changes to housing, financial support for renovations, and policies to improve housing standards. Multifactorial approaches, like those implemented in New Zealand and Seattle, have demonstrated significant health benefits, including reduced hospitalizations and asthma symptoms. Upgraded housing in informal settlements in El Salvador, Mexico, and Uruguay has improved child health, reduced parasitic infections, and enhanced overall life satisfaction. Economic analyses show that housing interventions, such as lead removal and insulation retrofitting, are cost-effective. For example, New Zealand’s insulation subsidy program yielded significant health system savings, with benefits outweighing costs by up to 6-to-1 for children and older adults. Similarly, replacing dirt floors with cement in Mexico improved child health and cognitive development, proving more cost-effective than cash transfer programs. Training is essential for implementing WHO’s housing and health guidelines. Health professionals need evidence-based training to target communities in substandard housing, while housing agencies require specialized training to identify and remediate housing problems. Cross-sector collaboration between health and housing professionals is crucial. WHO and its partners will provide technical assistance, training, and tools to support positive changes in health and housing policies at all levels. Dissemination of WHO’s guidelines will involve collaboration with international partners, including WHO offices, ministries of health, and other United Nations agencies.
